title: First Rheumatology Appointment: What to Ask and Expect

content:
Quick answer: A first rheumatology appointment usually includes questions about your symptoms and an examination. The team may arrange blood tests or scans, on the day or later. A diagnosis is not guaranteed at the first visit. Bring a medicines list, a short account of how symptoms affect you and your main questions. Follow your own clinic's instructions.

This guide helps adults prepare for an assessment, not diagnose their own arthritis. Clinics differ in who you see, which tests are needed and how results are sent. The appointment letter and your team's advice take priority over a general checklist.

Before the day: check the letter, not an assumed routine

Confirm the hospital, department, date and appointment format. A visit may be in person, by telephone or by video. Do not assume an old clinic location or a link from a previous appointment still applies. If you cannot attend, contact the service using the details on your letter rather than simply missing it.

NHS outpatient advice recommends preparing symptoms, medicines, allergies and questions. Check whether the clinic has asked for a questionnaire, blood test or other preparation beforehand. Ask the clinic if instructions about food, drink or medicines are unclear; do not stop treatment or fast just because you are going to rheumatology.

Tell the service in advance if you need an interpreter, communication support, help with mobility or a different appointment format. NHS Highland's current outpatient guidance gives the same practical starting point: contact the service on your letter about the support you need. For journey planning, see our separate hospital appointment-day guide.

A useful one-page summary to bring

  • Your main concern: what you most want help with, in your own words.
  • The pattern: when symptoms began, which joints are affected, swelling, stiffness and what has changed. Note good days as well as difficult days.
  • Everyday effects: examples such as dressing, sleep, work, walking or opening containers. Say what you can do and what needs help.
  • Medicines and allergies: include prescriptions, bought painkillers, vitamins and supplements, amounts where known, and anything you stopped because of a problem. Packets or clear label photographs can help.
  • Your questions: put the most important ones first. Bring relevant letters or results you have been asked to supply.

You do not need perfect records. A short, accurate account is more useful than trying to remember every symptom. If swelling comes and goes, you can ask whether dated photographs would help explain it. Keep personal health notes private rather than posting them in a public comment.

Who you might see and what you may be asked

Do not assume every appointment is with the named consultant. Gloucestershire Hospitals' rheumatology information describes assessment by a consultant, registrar or practitioner, including a nurse, physiotherapist or pharmacist. This is an example of one service, not a promise about every UK clinic.

The clinician may ask about current symptoms, previous health problems, family history, medicines and lifestyle. Mention symptoms outside the joints and how you are coping, rather than deciding in advance that something cannot matter. You can ask why a question is relevant. A stiffness duration or a symptom checklist on the internet cannot confirm a diagnosis.

You may be asked about students attending. The NHS says you can say no if you are not comfortable with trainees being present. You can also ask someone you trust to come with you. Agree whether you want them to take notes, help explain something or simply provide support.

The examination and possible tests

Wear clothes that make it reasonably easy to examine the affected area. The team may examine joints and movement and take observations such as blood pressure. Explain if an examination hurts or you need a break. Ask what is going to happen before a procedure if you are unsure.

Blood tests, X-rays or another scan may be appropriate, but not everybody needs every test. Gloucestershire's service explains that investigations may happen on the same day or later. Do not treat a local appointment-length estimate as the total time you will spend at hospital.

For suspected rheumatoid arthritis specifically, the NHS diagnosis guide explains that no blood test can definitively prove or rule it out. Tests such as ESR, CRP, rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP are interpreted alongside symptoms and examination. A positive antibody result alone is not a diagnosis; a negative result alone does not settle the question either. Different conditions need different investigations.

A clear plan matters even if there is no diagnosis yet

You may leave with a diagnosis, a working explanation awaiting results, a treatment discussion or a plan for care elsewhere. Some people do not need continuing rheumatology follow-up. That does not make their pain unimportant. If you are discharged, ask what the team thinks is causing the symptoms, who will help next and what changes should prompt reassessment.

If a medicine is proposed, ask about its purpose, benefits, risks, dose instructions and any monitoring before agreeing the plan. This article cannot decide which treatment you need or provide a dosing schedule. Ask the prescriber or pharmacist to explain anything that is unclear.

Before leaving: five questions worth answering

  1. What is the current explanation, and what remains uncertain?
  2. Which tests or treatments are next, and who arranges them?
  3. How and when will I hear about results, including normal results?
  4. Who should I contact if I have not heard by the agreed time or symptoms change?
  5. Will follow-up be booked, or do I need to contact the service myself?

Repeat the plan back in your own words and ask for important instructions in writing. Results arrangements vary: Gloucestershire, for example, says it does not routinely report normal blood tests and routine X-rays. The general NHS advice is to contact the hospital or clinic if results do not arrive as explained. Do not assume silence means everything is normal.

For telephone or video appointments, have your list ready, check contact details and equipment, and ask for the plan in writing afterwards. If you are offered patient-initiated follow-up, ask exactly how to request an appointment and what to do if the service does not respond. An advice line is not an emergency service.

When not to wait for the appointment

The NHS septic arthritis guide advises urgent medical help for sudden severe joint pain, swelling, difficulty moving a joint or joint pain with feeling unwell. A fever is not always present. Seek an urgent GP assessment or the local urgent-care service rather than waiting for a routine clinic date. In England use NHS 111 if you cannot get an urgent GP assessment. In Scotland contact your GP during opening hours or NHS 24 on 111 when you need urgent care and the practice is closed. NHS 111 Wales offers urgent advice; in Northern Ireland use your GP or local GP out-of-hours service. Call 999 for a life-threatening emergency.

Bring a blank record to your appointment

You can print a blank sheet to note symptoms, medicines and questions before your appointment. The sheets do not send your entries to this website and are not a treatment plan.

  • GP appointment symptom and medication tracker (PDF)
  • Flare-up daily log (PDF)
  • All symptom and flare printables

The new blank sheets are awaiting separate clinical review. Follow your existing care plan and the urgent-help advice in this guide.
